q: Based on the lot's total area and its frontage, how deep is the lot, in meters?
n: Dividing the 200-square-meter lot area by its 10-meter frontage gives a depth of 20 meters.

q: For the same R-1 building type, the National Building Code sets a 4.50-meter front setback, a local ordinance sets 5 meters, and the subdivision's own deed restrictions set 6 meters. Which figure applies?
n: When several regulations set different minimums for the same requirement, the most restrictive figure governs — here, the subdivision's 6-meter setback.

q: The National Building Code caps single-detached residential (R-1) buildings at three storeys, while a local ordinance caps the same building type at two storeys. Which limit governs?
o: Either applies equally, so it makes no difference
It is left to the Office of the Building Official to decide
n: Where a local ordinance imposes a stricter limit than the National Building Code, the stricter local standard controls — here, the two-storey cap.

q: Given that the rear of the lot borders the creekside area, what must legally be provided or maintained along that edge?
n: PD 1067 (Water Code of the Philippines) requires a mandatory easement along land bordering a creek, so an easement — not a promenade, esplanade, or the plain boundary line — applies here.

q: Because the site is flood-prone, the family patriarch — who is 65 years old — wants the finished floor raised 1 meter above natural grade, reached by a single-flight ramp. Following Batas Pambansa Blg. 344, what horizontal run, in meters, should that ramp have?
n: BP 344 caps ramp slope at 1:12, and factoring in the required level landing at the top of a 1-meter rise brings the total horizontal run to 13.5 meters.
